sourceName: Princeton Laboratory for Artificial Intelligence Research
title: Princeton researchers reconstruct viewed images from fMRI in about 15 seconds
friendlyTitle: Researchers turn brain scans into rough pictures within seconds
summary: A Princeton-led study used personalised fMRI training data and generative models to reconstruct rough versions of images a participant was viewing. Its fastest configuration produced recognisable semantic approximations about 15 seconds after viewing, rather than photographic copies.
friendlySummary: A Princeton study used an MRI scanner and AI to make a rough picture of what one person was looking at. The picture appeared about 15 seconds later and showed the main idea, not exact details.
whyItMatters: Faster decoding could support closed-loop neuroscience experiments and, eventually, carefully governed clinical research. This is not general mind reading: it requires an MRI scanner, about an hour of person-specific training and a participant looking at an image, which sharply limits immediate use and misuse.
friendlyWhyItMatters: This may help brain research react to a person’s signals during an experiment. It cannot read anyone’s thoughts from far away and needs expensive equipment plus personal training data.
